sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a broker should get paid from a signed commission line or from a spread. The Ultimate Jet Guide treats the spread as a fallback. If the seller refuses to pay and the buyer refuses too, you ask the seller for their number and take anything above $2 million. You then either write that into the agreement transparently, or run it through an intermediary company that puts the aircraft under contract at $2 million and presents it to the buyer at $2.1 million including commission [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:04:13] [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:05:04]. Sam Cutting goes further for freelance brokers: add the fee on top of the seller's price, or take payment yourself, pay the seller, and control the deal after face-to-face due diligence at the factory [QguZjBADFoA @ 00:01:45]. MarginCallMedia attacks exactly that model from the charter side. It calls the undisclosed markup the dominant compensation method and a blind premium that clients can neither verify nor negotiate, and says fee-only consultancies passing the operator's wholesale price through with zero markup are fracturing the industry [PWGk1rSbFhA @ 00:02:17]. The practical decision is whether your buyer will ask for two distinct numbers, because a broker who deflects that question gets read as hiding a spread.

Practitioners also split on how much weight a non-circumvention agreement can carry. Pryderi Podcast frames it as extremely valuable. Leads and relationships built up over months or years are worth real money, and an NCNDA makes going around the introducer a contractual violation that can expose the circumventing party to damages [rnUvOWiFpDQ @ 00:01:35]. Sam Cutting is blunter about enforcement. If you lack the money to take someone to court, and the other side is likely in another country, it is going to be difficult. Some attorneys may take a case on a no-win, no-fee basis, but only if you hold irrefutable evidence that you were cut out and the NCNDA was breached [QguZjBADFoA @ 00:02:07]. Cutting's real defense is structural rather than legal: get out of any situation with more than two entities. The Ultimate Jet Guide runs a third playbook built on information control instead of paper. When the seller won't sign a listing, strip tail and serial numbers from photos, cockpit shots, and spec sheets, and hold back maintenance reports. Then convert the deal to a one-page commission agreement naming the specific buyer before the floodgates open [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:01:24] [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:03:13]. Even Pryderi concedes the agreement is not always necessary.

On the size of the commission itself, the yacht and real estate camps pull in opposite directions. Christopher of Yacht Experts calls the typical 10% yacht fee part of an entrenched and inefficient model. The fee splits 5% per side, then employing licensed brokers take 50% of each side, so the working broker nets 2.5% while the employing broker adds very little if any value. Christopher's response was to form a licensed employing brokerage in Florida to run a more reasonable commission structure [NUVwWnSq3A0 @ 00:01:59]. Yacht Zero accepts the 10% and argues that the only thing more expensive than agreeing to it is not paying it, because unsold yachts lose value as every similar sale drops the price. Yacht Zero's leverage play is to make the listing broker carry professional photos, dockage, and boat show costs [oEXYo1_yeOU @ 00:00:10]. In residential, Think Real Estate reports that well over 90% of sellers still pay a buyer broker commission when the offer asks for it. The average buyer's agent fee slid only from 2.45% to 2.37%, about an $800 discount on a $1 million sale [wBbi84Xi1Bc @ 00:01:32]. Brandon Mulrenin agrees that sellers will still pay the vast majority of buyer agent commissions, and builds loan-structure workarounds only for the rare deal where the seller pays nothing [5YNeLidiqqU @ 00:15:26].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure The Ultimate Jet Guide describes is the transparent spread that evaporates in pre-buy. If you stand to make a hundred grand above the seller's $2 million and squawks force a hundred-grand price reduction, you get paid nothing [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:04:39]. The same speaker warns against letting a referring broker or pilot take control of the conversation. When someone asks for 50 grand and there is only 50 grand of commission in the deal, you pin them to an exact number. You then negotiate toward 10 grand if they only brought the buyer, or 25 if they are helping get the deal across the line [1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:07:46]. Sam Cutting describes the chain-length trap in terms of payout odds. The broker who introduced a broker to the broker who is direct to the buyer or seller has slim chances of getting paid, while the one who connects buyer and seller directly fares far better [QguZjBADFoA @ 00:02:30]. MarginCallMedia shows the downstream cost of sub-brokering. Every layer quietly takes its own margin, and squeezed operators respond by trimming crew rest, hiring less experienced pilots, or delaying crucial maintenance [PWGk1rSbFhA @ 00:02:50]. Every extra hand in the chain shrinks the check and raises the odds that it never clears.

At closing, the commission and the down payment both ride on wires, and Family Split Strategy describes how they get stolen. Hackers break into the weakest inbox in the email chain, often a small realtor, inspector, or insurance office working on home Wi-Fi or in a coffee shop. They read who the title company and buyer are, register a lookalike domain, and build a matching website in an hour or two. Then they email fake wiring instructions complete with logos and a phone number that rings to the scammer [DZe5D7_TCDA @ 00:04:08] [DZe5D7_TCDA @ 00:06:22]. The fix they teach costs close to zero. Send a test wire of $1 to $1,000 and confirm receipt by walking into the real office or calling a number you looked up yourself. Then send the full balance to the same unchanged account. Title companies should run the same test before they release a commission to a realtor [DZe5D7_TCDA @ 00:12:30]. Hauseit adds a verbal check: call the attorney you have actually met and read the account and routing numbers aloud. Once a fraudulent wire lands, there is not much you can do to remedy it [KrsoinTC_10 @ 00:01:37]. The recovery window Family Split describes is narrow: file with IC3 and push the financial fraud kill chain, usually within 72 hours.

Slower failures come from paperwork and logistics rather than theft. Equity Real Estate warns that any missing or wrong field on the commission disbursement and wire instructions form can hold up the check. The agent fills in every field, especially the email addresses. The agent then coaches the title or escrow side to list the exact wire amount, their bank name, and contact information, and touches base a day or two before closing so the commission lands by direct deposit within 24 hours [mVFdzEqW2M4 @ 00:01:06]. Giuseppe Battaglioli has seen buyers hit daily wire limits at banks with no local branch. One client had to drive to Kansas to get a cashier's check before closing [YtS2MXC9Bps @ 00:01:07]. Lauren's escrow rule is just as rigid. As the neutral third party, escrow acts only on mutually agreed instructions, so contract changes must reach escrow as written amendments within three days of acceptance [IK3LgAFr-QQ @ 00:02:05]. Steve, the lender on Brandon Mulrenin's episode, hit the timing trap on a live loan. The appraisal came back exactly at contract price, which killed a late request to raise the price and add concessions [5YNeLidiqqU @ 00:15:11]. That is why any commission-funding concession has to be written into the original offer.

callout.title: Hold Specs And Money Until These Four Checks Clear
callout.body: Each check below comes from a loss, a dead deal, or a delayed payout that practitioners reported firsthand. If any check fails, stop sending identifying details and stop releasing funds.
items: No signed agreement saying how you get paid means no tail numbers, serial numbers, or maintenance reports go out; send only a scrubbed spec sheet [The Ultimate Jet Guide — 1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:05:44].

If more than two entities sit between you and the principal, or an NCNDA arrives with 14 intermediaries, walk away instead of chasing the fee [Sam Cutting - Red Flags Verification — QguZjBADFoA @ 00:00:42].

No full wire goes out until a small test wire is confirmed through a phone number you looked up yourself or in person at the office, never a number taken from the email [Family Split Strategy — DZe5D7_TCDA @ 00:09:23].
No closing date is treated as locked until both sides of the disbursement form are complete and the funding entity has been contacted a day or two ahead [Equity Real Estate — mVFdzEqW2M4 @ 00:01:21].

chapters.pull_quote: "Again, the most important thing is that you have something in writing that says how you're going to get paid before you start sending specs." Attributed to The Ultimate Jet Guide (1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:05:44).
action_checklist: When you ask a seller about an off-market sale, also ask whether they will pay a commission and get the percentage agreed verbally, such as 6% or 4%. Then send a one-page agreement naming the buyer [The Ultimate Jet Guide — 1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:02:49].

Ask every broker, pilot, or management company in the deal how they are getting paid, and refuse to move forward until they give an exact dollar amount [The Ultimate Jet Guide — 1ILeO7AapJM @ 00:06:29].

On charter deals, show the operator's wholesale cost and your advisory fee as separate line items so a client's two-number question cannot sink your credibility [MarginCallMedia — PWGk1rSbFhA @ 00:01:59].

Settle buyer agent compensation and seller concessions in the original offer, before the appraisal is ordered. If the buyer is short on cash, use a lender credit, such as moving from 6.125% to 6.625% for a 1% credit [Brandon Mulrenin — 5YNeLidiqqU @ 00:05:26].

Tell every buyer and seller to send a small test wire, confirm receipt by phone or walk-in at the real office, and then wire the full balance to the same unchanged account [Family Split Strategy — DZe5D7_TCDA @ 00:08:35].

Fill out every field on your side of the commission disbursement and wire instructions form. Coach the title or escrow side to add the exact wire amount, bank name, and contact information [Equity Real Estate — mVFdzEqW2M4 @ 00:00:51].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I choose a brokerage or build my own firm, recruit and retain agents, and organize its basic operating structure?
chapters.title: Building and Running a Brokerage
chapters.subtitle: Boutique versus franchise firms, brokerage-selection questions, commercial brokerage entry, independent-firm startup, recruiting and retention, AI-assisted growth, pipeline basics, and exclusive listing agreements
chapters.executive_summary: Brokerage owners agree that the agent makes the company. They recruit experienced producers, sell value instead of the cheapest split, and scale slowly, because brokerages fail from carrying too many costs too soon. Garth Ward seeded Park Place with a coffee-shop event where 10+ agents signed on day one, then grew to 137 agents and 4 offices. Even so, he ran at about 10% margins and rebuilt pricing from a 90/10 split with a $15K cap to 70/30 with a $500 transaction fee and a 2.25% servicing fee. Jim Remley abandoned new-agent seminars after 87% attrition and switched to targeting $2-10M producers. Joe Mendoza calls a $500 flat fee a model for going broke without ancillary revenue. Practitioners split on boutique versus franchise, where franchise fees run 3% to 8% off the top. They also split on whether social media or prospecting calls drive revenue.

key_metrics.label: Brokerage Profit Margin at Scale
key_metrics.context: Garth Ward's reported margins while running Park Place at multi-office scale. He says the model only truly works at about 1,000 agents.

key_metrics.label: New-Agent Recruiting Attrition
key_metrics.context: Jim Remley's results from monthly two-hour recruiting seminars for new licensees. These results drove the pivot to experienced $2-10M producers.

key_metrics.label: Business Sale Cycle and Capacity
key_metrics.value: 7-month average sale, 5 deals at a time
key_metrics.context: Christine McDannell's boutique business-brokerage throughput, run on a 15-touch follow-up cadence.

key_metrics.label: Franchise Fee Off the Top
key_metrics.value: 3% to 6%, up to 8% of every commission
key_metrics.context: Franchise fees the Signature Properties founders paid before the office split, at the franchises they worked for prior to going boutique.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who opened a shop agrees on the first prerequisite: owning a brokerage is a separate trade. Kyle Handy calls it an entirely different ball game, not agent work multiplied. It carries heavier legal and tax consequences, and the broker may answer for dozens or even hundreds of agents [QqzqH1glUuA @ 00:01:59]. The entry ticket is a broker's license. Requirements vary by state and cover education classes, industry experience and an exam, and without the license nobody carries agents under them [QqzqH1glUuA @ 00:04:17]. Ben Eger spells out what that license puts on the owner's desk. The supervising broker oversees licensed work, records, advertising and entrusted funds, and no office policy erases that responsibility. Earnest money sits in trust with an accurate ledger, separate from operating revenue. Paying office expenses out of a buyer's deposit is conversion, not merely commingling [DPj-ieo_sSM @ 00:01:40]. Dee Kumar adds the remaining baseline. Escrow funds are never commingled or converted, and every ad carries the broker ID and license number, with no blind ads. There is also a hard antitrust line against colluding, fixing prices, allocating markets or forcing tie-in agreements [V5gUCAcegsY @ 00:04:15]. Both instructors stress that commissions are negotiable and not fixed by law, so every split and fee is open to design [V5gUCAcegsY @ 00:02:43].

The second point of agreement is that agents are the brokerage's real customers, and experienced producers are the inventory worth chasing. Bob Knakal opens the commercial panel with a line the other founders echo: the agent makes the company [0u9CyKG6vj4 @ 00:00:00]. Jim Remley learned this the expensive way. The early model of monthly two-hour seminars for new licensees produced an 87% attrition rate and kept roughly 1 in 10 recruits [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:08:38]. Remley then pivoted to agents with more than two years in the business and $2 to $10 million in production. That shift carried the firm to 17 offices [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:10:00]. Garth Ward narrows the target further to the on-the-bubble agent: $1.5 to $3.5 million in volume and $50K to $120K GCI, poached from smaller independent brokerages [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:17:01]. Ward also notes where most shops stall. Most brokerages sit around 4 agents, few reach 10, and most plateau near 30 agents per office [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:03:41]. Tim Garrity's first roughly 10 agents came through relationships. After that, better splits, a cap system and a handbook co-written with agents carried recruiting [2WIql7qBDoY @ 00:11:06]. The shared lesson is to recruit people who already produce and then keep them close.

The third consensus is that owners win on value delivered, not on the cheapest split. Remley is blunt: top agents generally don't work for the lowest-cost office, and competing on lowest cost is a fallacy. That is why the model charges a $50 to $75 monthly tech-stack fee instead of racing to zero [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:34:16]. Brandon Mulrenin applies the same test from the agent's chair. Compensation has to line up with the value exchange between broker and agent, and high-fee, low-value, broker-centric firms are the ones to avoid [R_uWZH6c9lI @ 00:12:56]. Joe Mendoza paid more than $200K to the house, the broker-owner and the franchise in a GCI year north of $1M, yet spoke to the broker-owner once. He lands on one rule: if your benefits exceed the cost, that's not a bad deal [VcNeWYSFiDE @ 00:03:45]. The flip side is cost discipline inside the owner's own books. Handy warns that brokerages fail because they scale too quickly and carry too many costs. The plan has to project income, show break-even, and budget for negative cash flow for at least a few years, starting with a handful of people or even a family [QqzqH1glUuA @ 00:03:40].

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Garth Ward's launch is the most detailed playbook on record. In under a week, Ward pulled market data, cold-called a couple hundred agents with low or no production, and rented a coffee shop for a $200 minimum buy-in. About 15 showed up, printed contracts sat on the tables, and over 10 agents signed on day one [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:06:27]. Co-hosted events with lenders and title reps, such as Facebook ads training, pushed Park Place to 30 agents in four to five months [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:08:28]. Every later recruit got a custom presentation and sales deck, because the team treated every agent appointment like a million-dollar listing [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:14:03]. The agent-referral incentive paid a recruiting agent a portion of the recruit's commission until cap, every year the recruit stayed, and it drove about 25% of growth [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:22:13]. Indeed ads added 20+ agents in a year [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:22:45]. Remley turns chasing into attracting. The target is 3 to 5 agents a month calling in, fed by touching the database 20 to 50 times a year, and experienced agents are never closed, only offered an open door [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:14:32]. George Pino recruits with a 100% split on the first couple of deals, education-based pitches and referral bonuses for agents who bring in hires [0u9CyKG6vj4 @ 00:20:10].

The pricing math is where launches live or die. Ward opened with a 90/10 split, a monthly fee, a $15K cap and a $150 transaction fee, and calls that model not viable [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:32:22]. The rebuilt structure ran a 70/30 split, a $500 transaction fee that includes transaction management, and a 2.25% servicing fee on every deal regardless of cap [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:33:54]. Even then, Ward reports profit margins around 10% [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:33:14]. He pegs the real economics at roughly 1,000 agents, or about 20 locations of 50 agents each [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:13:30]. Mendoza served as state broker for a flat-fee firm and calls roughly $500 per transaction a model for going broke unless ancillary title, lending and insurance revenue fills the gap [VcNeWYSFiDE @ 00:10:04]. On the franchise side, Jesse Ebner's team saw 3%, 6% and up to 8% taken off the top of every commission. That came before office splits of 70/30, 50/50 or up to 90/10 [6cCUTLOmNIE @ 00:01:16]. Keeping that money local let the boutique donate almost $60,000 to 12 nonprofits in one year [6cCUTLOmNIE @ 00:02:25]. Remley's parity list is the floor every model still has to fund: mobile website, company email, CRM and CMA/AVM, with an AI tech stack as the differentiator [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:32:59].

On the deal side, the mechanics come down to follow-up cadence and response speed. Christine McDannell runs 15 touch points, reaching out by call, text and email about five times each, every few days. McDannell holds only 5 deals at a time and averages a sale in 7 months [7jkOz9WXEh8 @ 00:22:08]. Sellers pay a $15K to $20K deposit credited toward the success fee, backed by a 90-day guarantee. If no solid LOI from a qualified, capitalized buyer arrives within 90 days flat, the deposit comes back [7jkOz9WXEh8 @ 00:09:54]. The buyer database has lived in Zoho CRM for 5 years [7jkOz9WXEh8 @ 00:39:55]. Eddie Gonzalez's team, half of whom trained at the Ritz-Carlton, holds to the 15-minute callback rule [0u9CyKG6vj4 @ 00:12:37]. The Toolnest Explained pipeline gives the board its structure: new lead, contacting, qualified, proposal sent, negotiation, won and lost. Each card moves as calls and quotes happen, so deals never go completely cold [B4H8Hy41Myg @ 00:01:38]. Tim Garrity's database of about 7,000 gets quarterly neighborhood reports covering listings, solds, days on market and price trend. It also gets a monthly newsletter with one blog post, three to four listings and one lifestyle piece, which takes an hour a month to keep as a solid drip campaign [2WIql7qBDoY @ 00:22:08].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among practitioners is where the money goes after every closing. The Jesse Ebner hosts worked at two franchises and two boutiques before launching Signature Properties in 2017, and they chose not to franchise because the franchise takes 3% at one firm, 6% at another and 'all the way up to eight percent' off the top of every commission, before the office split even lands [6cCUTLOmNIE @ 00:01:16]. They kept that money local, bought tools their agents actually use, and donated almost $60,000 to 12 nonprofits last year. Joe Mendoza makes the same math from the agent chair. In his year above $1M GCI he paid more than $200K to the house, the broker-owner and the franchise fee, yet spoke to the broker-owner once, so his rule is to stay only if the benefits exceed the cost [VcNeWYSFiDE @ 00:03:07]. Mendoza also found boutique pay 'loosey-goosey' as an REO firm VP, and joined eXp in 2020. Garth Ward took the same exit after scaling Park Place to 137 agents, deciding in about three weeks and adding roughly 150 agents and 25 states on eXp revenue share [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:47:31]. Tim Garrity holds the opposite line. He frames eXp and KW as McDonald's against 'Tim's Burger Shop,' a brokerage built on customer service, paperless workflows and texting [2WIql7qBDoY @ 00:24:00].

Practitioners also split on which agents to build around. Jim Remley tried the new-agent route first. Monthly two-hour seminars produced 87% attrition and kept roughly 1 in 10 recruits [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:08:38]. He pivoted to agents with more than two years in the business and $2 to $10 million in production, which carried the firm to 17 offices. He also warns against trying to 'close' those agents; open the door and stack benefits over time instead. Garth Ward launched the opposite way. He pulled market data and cold-called a couple hundred agents with low or no production, rented a coffee shop for a $200 minimum and laid printed contracts on the tables. More than 10 agents signed on day one, and nearly all became top producers [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:06:27]. Ward's later sweet spot is the 'on the bubble' agent doing $1.5 to $3.5 million in volume and $50K to $120K GCI, poached from smaller independents [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:17:01]. Kyle Handy splits the difference. New agents are easier to recruit and more loyal, while experienced agents bring a book of business but are harder to land. So most brokerages start with a mix and use administrative services and subsidized education as the hook [QqzqH1glUuA @ 00:10:14].

The split itself is the loudest disagreement. US Realty Training calls 50/50 'no bueno,' treats 70/30 as reasonable and notes smaller shops offering 90/10, but warns that 90 of nothing is still nothing [4LntMyEuBXE @ 00:03:19]. Amanda Fesalani of Designed For Agents defends deeper splits when the support is real: the more a brokerage provides at no cost, the deeper the split. Splits run from 60/40 and 70/30 down to 50/50 on teams and as low as 40/60. Meanwhile, 100% shops charging $250 to $500 per transaction often leave a new agent alone with a 3 a.m. or 7 a.m. emergency [Vbv1TkWvBD8 @ 00:03:59]. Fesalani expects most successful agents to settle into a hybrid model long term. Brandon Mulrenin runs a 100% model and lays out the menu as 50/50 with no cap, 100%, or 70/30 with a cap. He insists compensation must track the value exchange between broker and agent [R_uWZH6c9lI @ 00:12:56]. Garth Ward shows the owner-side result. Park Place opened at 90/10 with a monthly fee, a $15K cap and a $150 transaction fee, and found it unviable. It ended at 70/30, a $500 transaction fee including transaction management, and a 2.25% servicing fee on every deal regardless of cap [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:32:22].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first economics check is that owning the brokerage may pay less than selling. Kyle Handy tells new brokers to expect negative cash flow 'for at least a few years.' He states flatly that brokerages fail because they scale too quickly and carry too many costs [QqzqH1glUuA @ 00:03:40]. Jim Remley plans for two years of reduced personal production when opening an office, because the owner's own deals carry the build [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:08:08]. Garth Ward lived the numbers at scale. At about 80 agents he hired managers, a CEO and a front desk, the raised fees barely covered staff, and margins ran around 10% [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:33:14]. By his math the model only works near 1,000 agents, roughly 20 locations of 50 agents each. Multi-state licensing would have taken about 16 years to reach 15 states. Legal exposure compounds it: two lawsuits in four years cost just under $200K combined because an entity cannot represent itself [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:38:15]. Ward also warns that Zillow leads worked at 50/50 are team income, not brokerage profit. Buyout offers that once came in at 3x net on a three-year earnout now look closer to 2x. His conclusion is blunt: a high-producing agent will make more money than a brokerage owner.

Undercharging is the most repeated pricing mistake. Joe Mendoza served as state broker for a flat-fee firm charging about $500 per transaction. He calls it a model for going broke unless title, lending and insurance revenue fill the gap; he was micromanaged there and resigned [VcNeWYSFiDE @ 00:09:32]. At Keller Williams he recruited agents and still earned 'zero' because profit share depends on the office being profitable. Garth Ward admits Park Place undercharged early and ran an undialed brand that forced a full niche rebrand. He also found that building proprietary tech cost more than the fees it replaced [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:11:48]. Jim Remley rejects the race to the bottom entirely. Parity items like a mobile site, company email, CRM and CMA/AVM sit behind a $50 to $75 monthly tech fee, and top agents generally do not work for the lowest-cost office [YKfvldXPHWw @ 00:34:16]. From the other side of the desk, Brandon Mulrenin warns agents that broker-centric firms bury costs in printing, color printing, technology, broker review, E&O, office and desk fees. Then they hit agents with surprise month-end bills [R_uWZH6c9lI @ 00:07:18]. Mulrenin also calls payouts that take weeks unacceptable; 24 to 48 hours by direct deposit is the standard.

Deal-side failures cluster around time, ego and bad numbers. Christine McDannell says the hard part is holding the whole deal together. McDannell watched a COVID lockdown kill a multi-million-dollar sale the day before closing, which is the origin of the rule that time kills deals [7jkOz9WXEh8 @ 00:12:10]. McDannell also fields sellers anchored on AI valuations. One claimed $5M on $150K net after a Claude run, a business McDannell put at about $900K max. Another seller invented $6M on roughly $50K to $120K net [7jkOz9WXEh8 @ 00:33:07]. A Bay Area salon seller took a full-price, all-cash offer from a buyer who pulled a HELOC, then balked at a three-year, 50-mile non-compete and walked. The countermeasure is a $15K to $20K deposit credited toward the success fee, which screens seller commitment, backed by a 90-day LOI guarantee. Inside the office, Garth Ward warns that skipping an early manager hire and re-routing agents to managers later damaged culture [OFzI2gK-nps @ 00:29:15]. Brandon Mulrenin reports agents losing deals while waiting a week to hear back from their broker. That support gap pushes producers out the door [R_uWZH6c9lI @ 00:04:07].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I source off-market opportunities, approach owners and family offices, exchange initial deal information, and track opportunities in a CRM?
chapters.title: Off-Market Outreach and Deal-Pipeline Management
chapters.subtitle: Cold email, owner-outreach sequences, live property calls, family-office capital conversations and investment perspectives, CIM exchange, and HubSpot, Zoho, and Close pipelines
chapters.executive_summary: Off-market deal flow comes from owners who already lean toward selling, reached through stacked, low-pressure touches and tracked in a disciplined pipeline. Wolf of Main Street's Michael Lucvich and Paul Macaluso agree never to ask an owner outright whether they want to sell; Nick Abraham opens with a valuation offer instead, and Lucvich offers a guide or prospectus. Mechanics are specific: Abraham builds lists by headcount in Apollo, scrapes via Export List at about $50 per search, and sends from secondary inboxes in Smartlead; Lucvich runs a seven-touch email, call, social, and handwritten-letter sequence with sub-60-word plain-text emails. LoCasa reached about 5 of 28 owners in a couple of hours. Practitioners split on the low-commitment ask, on whether a letter should precede the call, and on who qualifies leads before the buyer gets involved.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Find Owners Already Leaning In, Ask Small, Stack Touches
paragraphs: Across business acquisitions and real estate, the operators converge on one rule: hunt for owners who already lean toward a sale instead of trying to talk anyone into one. Michael Lucvich of Wolf of Main Street builds an entire outreach machine around that premise, telling buyers to stop convincing and to drop the opt-in barrier with a lead magnet [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:00:44]. Brandon Thomas, after roughly five years of buying houses and apartments for cash and creatively, names sellers who need to move quickly for personal reasons as the best targets [vOB7Te243ew @ 00:00:20]. The second shared rule is never to lead with the blunt question. Paul Macaluso warns that the moment you ask an owner whether they are looking to sell, you have already lost [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:02:44], and Lucvich ends every email with a single yes/no offer of a guide or prospectus rather than a request for a call. Nick Abraham reaches the same soft entry from the business side, asking owners whether they would be open to getting the business valued, on the logic that everyone wants to sell their business [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:06:25]. The first ask stays small, specific, and easy to accept; price talk waits until the owner raises a hand.

The second point of agreement is that a single channel rarely carries the deal; operators stack touches and let each one warm up the next. Paul Macaluso opens by saying 'I don't cold call': every phone conversation follows a certified letter, and that sequencing is what Macaluso credits for six- and seven-figure contracts [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:00:00]. Lucvich runs the same order inside a seven-touch sequence: plain-text email, call, an email that references the call, call plus social outreach, another email, a handwritten letter, and a final call about a week after the letter lands, with touches spaced two to three days apart [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:02:25]. Brandon Thomas works a wider real estate funnel of driving for dollars, direct mail, cold calls and texts, wholesalers, bird dogs, probate attorneys, pocket listings, and social media, and has personally sent hundreds of postcards, mailers, and handwritten letters [vOB7Te243ew @ 00:02:33]. Rachel of LoCasa shows why volume matters on the phone: roughly 28 properties dialed in one session produced about five conversations, around 20 percent, and roughly three maybes, all inside a couple of hours [Fug5C3kFHsA @ 00:18:40]. Nobody in this group treats outreach as one email blast; the deal surfaces from persistence across mail, phone, inbox, and social, logged and repeated on schedule.

The baseline prerequisites are confidentiality, real numbers, and a tracked pipeline. Macaluso offers a signed confidentiality agreement up front, promises a formal number within seven days, and asks only for the rent roll and trailing-twelve-month P&L, explaining that the goal is a strong offer rather than a lowball [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:00:35]. Jim Loeffler makes the same point on the business-sale side: every buyer signs an NDA before receiving the confidential information memorandum [aUN31sD75T0 @ 00:02:31], and leaks panic employees, customers, and vendors [UMCbZCe6qzw @ 00:03:49]. Abraham and Frankie Finance both qualify on hard figures, trailing-twelve-month revenue and EBITDA for Abraham, seller's discretionary earnings rather than revenue for the family-office buyer. Once a lead is real, the CRM operators insist it lives in a pipeline with stages, owners, and dates. Tutorial Toolkit stresses that the close date keeps urgency alive and the owner field enforces accountability [Sna6rbbuzww @ 00:01:49], while Hema Glory's HubSpot build assigns a probability to every stage so the board shows weighted value. The practical consensus: protect the seller's secret, ask for the two or three documents that price the deal, and log every conversation against a stage, an owner, and a deadline.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Nick Abraham's business-acquisition stack starts with the list. Revenue filters in Apollo and ZoomInfo are unreliable because the figures are estimated from headcount, so Abraham uses the average employee headcount of current or ideal investments as the north star and screens the rest on the back end [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:01:09]. A free Apollo account handles general lists, Ocean builds niche lookalike lists, and Export List scrapes a pasted Apollo search URL for roughly $50 per search before the company list goes back into Apollo [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:04:22]. Sending never happens from the primary domain, which wrecks deliverability; Abraham orders inboxes through Instantly's done-for-you service and runs them inside Smartlead, since self-setup demands DNS knowledge [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:05:04]. Lucvich adds that reputation travels upstream from mailbox to domain, so the sender should be a generic M&A brand along the lines of 'blue keyboard capital'; an A/B test against lookalike domains showed no difference, the actual buyer is revealed only after the owner opts in, and legal footers stay on every send [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:07:10]. Lucvich also keeps about 50 percent spare inbox capacity and rotates out boxes with high bounce rates. Abraham's guiding principle is a bare-bones minimum viable campaign: prove it works cheaply, then reinvest.

Lucvich caps every email under 60 words, plain text with no links or images, keeps the sender's name and firm out of the body to dodge spam flagging, and closes on one yes/no question offering a guide or prospectus [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:04:05]. Abraham's template runs: hey first name, we're looking to buy companies in a given industry and location, happened to come across your company, would you be open to getting your business valued. On the phone, Lucvich uses a permission opener, 'This is a cold call... Do you have a minute?', or the no-oriented 'is this a bad time?', and double-dials whenever nobody picks up [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:09:06]. Macaluso's ten-step real estate call references the certified letter ('Did you receive it?'), mentions driving the property last month, states 'I'm not a broker... a buyer' making an unsolicited offer, offers a signed confidentiality agreement, commits to a formal number within seven days, requests only the rent roll and T12, recaps next steps, and turns a cold 'no' into 'not yet' by staying in touch [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:00:35]. Abraham routes interested email repliers to an SDR, intern, or South American Upwork hire who phones them for trailing-twelve-month revenue and EBITDA; undersized leads go on file for a check-back in one to two years [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:06:51].

Lucvich runs calls through Trellus, with no affiliation, registers numbers with the Free Caller Registry, uses local numbers, and finds one number enough for 20 to 30 calls a day [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:11:24]. Letters are AI-robot handwritten and carry a phone number, while QR codes do not work; on social the word is 'partnership', never 'buy'. Market size sets cadence: small markets get more touches, double-dials, texts, and voicemails, while large markets get a parallel dialer and fewer touches [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:15:24]. Every live lead then lands in a pipeline. Hema Glory's HubSpot build starts stage setup with probabilities: new lead 10 percent, call booked 20, call completed 40, qualified 50, proposal sent 60, proposal accepted 70, contract sent 90, with closed won reserved for when the customer has actually paid [zWRMFLm_we4 @ 00:01:38]. The free plan allows only one pipeline, and conditional required fields can force amount and close date at intake and a proposal upload before 'proposal accepted'. Close supports multiple pipelines, drags deals left to mark won and right to mark lost, and flips a 'needs attention' toggle that flags inactive deals or deals stalled in a stage [4XHqzQ8JPzk @ 00:01:53]. Back in HubSpot, the Kanban view rolls those probabilities into a weighted amount across the board.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The low-commitment ask splits the cold-outreach camp three ways. Nick Abraham runs the bluntest version: a short email that says the sender is looking to buy companies in a given industry or location, names the target business, and asks whether the owner would be open to getting the business valued, on the logic that everyone wants to sell their business [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:06:25]. Michael Lucvich of Wolf of Main Street refuses to put a call or even the firm name in the first touch. Those emails stay under 60 words, carry no links or images, and close on a single yes/no question offering a guide or prospectus, with the buyer revealed only after the owner opts in [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:05:54]. Paul Macaluso goes the other direction on identity. On the phone, Macaluso states plainly that the caller is not a broker but a buyer making an unsolicited offer, offers a signed confidentiality agreement up front, promises a formal number within 7 days, and asks only for the rent roll and the T12 P&L [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:00:35]. The common thread is that nobody asks the owner outright whether they want to sell. Macaluso says that asking that question means you have already lost [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:02:44].

Channel order is the second fault line. Macaluso opens with the line I don't cold call. A certified letter lands first, and the phone call references it with did you receive it and I drove the property last month, a sequence Macaluso credits for 6 to 7 figure contracts [Cn4V6pWhbMk @ 00:00:00]. Lucvich builds a seven-touch sequence instead: plain-text email, call, email referencing the call, call plus social, email, AI-robot handwritten letter, then a call about a week after the letter arrives. Touches are spaced 2 to 3 days apart, each one points back to the last, and the receptionist is addressed by name [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:02:25]. Lucvich also scales intensity by market size. Small markets get more touches, double-dials, texts, and voicemails, while large markets get a parallel dialer and fewer touches. Rachel at LoCasa skips the warm-up entirely and dials listed and lead-source properties live. On the first call, Rachel pitches subject-to, seller finance, and wraps, and sends an LOI when the numbers work [Fug5C3kFHsA @ 00:12:39]. Brandon Thomas treats cold calling and texting as one lane among seven, pulling tired-landlord and inherited-property lists while running driving for dollars, direct mail, probate, pocket listings, and Facebook Marketplace alongside it [vOB7Te243ew @ 00:03:11].

On the capital and relationship side, practitioners split on whether to pay intermediaries or go direct. Frankie Finance lists four parallel sourcing channels for a family office deploying a 20% private deal reserve: brokers and BizBuySell, where sellers pay 8 to 12% fees, plus search funds, direct cold outreach, and networks. The targets are businesses with $400 to 900K of SDE bought at 2.5 to 4x [1PRKZu79Zg4 @ 00:12:43]. Andrew LeBaron skips paid listings and works referral gatekeepers. LeBaron takes business brokers and M&A attorneys out to eat, works CPAs who will soft circle deals, and mines title companies such as Commonwealth for names after closing. LeBaron calls RIAs the toughest nut, a slow marathon [LlJs_vz0sPs @ 00:00:55]. Inside the family-office world, the Centimillionaire Strategies panel runs on peer flow. Shane shares deal flow with other offices and sources through founders, while Cliff Oberlin vets deals in YPO forums of 8 and spins up SPV club deals [60V2lsbfZos @ 00:08:40]. Cresset co-founder Eric pushes back on the wirehouse version of that relationship. Eric describes a wirehouse advisor who was compensated on Eric's own mortgage and calls that arrangement a conflict rather than an advantage [QDcDBGMiDtQ @ 00:13:31].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Deliverability is where most cold-email operators burn their first month. Lucvich tells a cautionary story of roughly 15,000 emails pushed in a single week from a .edu address, which ended in a ban. The Wolf of Main Street rule since then is that reputation travels upstream from mailbox to domain, so outreach runs on a generic M&A domain like blue keyboard capital [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:05:19]. Nick Abraham makes the same point from the agency side. Never send from the primary domain, because it ruins deliverability. Order inboxes through Instantly's done-for-you service, run them in Smartlead, and self-build only if someone on the team knows DNS [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:05:04]. Lucvich adds a capacity rule: keep about 50% spare inbox capacity and rotate out boxes with high bounce rates. On the phone side, the rule is to register numbers with the Free Caller Registry, dial from local numbers, and expect one number to handle 20 to 30 calls a day [FZ98S2zrji0 @ 00:12:27]. Brandon Thomas flags the residential equivalent. Check the Do Not Call list before dialing tired landlords, avoid spam texts, and never get aggressive with or harass owners found through driving for dollars [vOB7Te243ew @ 00:03:52].

The second trap is a pipeline stuffed with deals that were never real. Abraham warns that Apollo and ZoomInfo revenue filters are estimated from headcount, so the list has to be built from the average headcount of current or ideal investments and filtered on the back end [Wdk1N79_WyM @ 00:01:09]. Booking calls straight from email replies fills calendars with businesses that are far too small. That is why, in Abraham's process, an SDR, intern, or Upwork hire phones every interested lead for trailing-12-month revenue and EBITDA first. LoCasa's live session shows the raw math. About 28 properties were called and about 5 owners reached, a 20% contact rate, which produced roughly 3 maybes in a couple of hours [Fug5C3kFHsA @ 00:18:40]. The dead ends are specific. One owner at 670 wants the loan out of their name, and on a 350 listing a relocation company blocks creative financing [Fug5C3kFHsA @ 00:16:43]. On the business-acquisition side, Frankie Finance treats a seller who refuses a 10 to 20% seller note as a warning sign and flags 60% of revenue from one client as concentration risk. Frankie Finance also pays about $15K for a quality-of-earnings review, citing an example where $80K of one-time gains were hidden in the numbers [1PRKZu79Zg4 @ 00:16:31].

Confidentiality and stage hygiene decide whether a live deal survives to close. Jim Loeffler warns that leaks panic employees, customers, and vendors. CIM inputs therefore move through a secure Dropbox link rather than email, and the CFO, controller, or bookkeeper is either read in or handed a consultant or process-improvement cover story [UMCbZCe6qzw @ 00:03:49]. Loeffler also resets timelines. Every buyer signs an NDA, and a sale takes a year or two, not six months, which is why the CIM doubles as an improvement roadmap and a pre-built data room [aUN31sD75T0 @ 00:04:04]. In the CRM, the failure is optimistic staging. Hema Glory's rule is that closed won applies only once the customer has paid. Conditional required fields block a deal from reaching proposal accepted until a proposal is uploaded [zWRMFLm_we4 @ 00:03:59]. Close's needs-attention toggle surfaces deals that have gone inactive or stalled in a stage, and the pipeline can draft the follow-up email from there [4XHqzQ8JPzk @ 00:01:53]. The Centimillionaire Strategies moderator puts the whole funnel in perspective. Fairbridge closes on about 1% of the transactions it reviews, even while deploying billions, and rejects 100% LTV, zero-equity deals outright.

chapters.question_prompt: Which earnings measure and multiple should I use to evaluate a business, and how do SaaS characteristics and financing terms affect the proposed transaction?
chapters.title: Business Valuation: Earnings, Multiples, and Deal Structure
chapters.subtitle: SDE, EBIT, EBITDA, add-backs, net profit versus cash flow, e-commerce valuations, SaaS valuation levers and exit planning, SBA financing, seller notes, earnouts, and rollovers
chapters.executive_summary: Brokers, lower-middle-market advisors, SaaS specialists and a valuation professor converge on one formula: normalized earnings times a risk-adjusted multiple. Under roughly $500K-$1M of earnings, buyers price Seller's Discretionary Earnings (SDE) at about 2-4x; above that, adjusted EBITDA takes over and multiples climb with size, from 3-5x at $500K-$1M EBITDA to 6-10x at $5-10M and 12x-plus above $10M. Owner dependence, customer concentration, trend, recurring revenue and clean books move the multiple. Lenders cap price through SBA 7(a) rules: tax returns as source of truth, 10% buyer injection, DSCR floors of 1.25 versus a stated 1.5 lender appetite. Sharp splits remain on personal add-backs such as vehicles and phones, on juicing trailing earnings before a sale, and on whether headline price or cash at closing defines the real deal.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Main Street brokers and lower-middle-market advisors start from the same arithmetic: normalized earnings times a multiple, with risk deciding where the multiple lands. Shep Campbell of Deal Street, who values businesses every week, frames value as earnings, multiple and risk, and insists buyers purchase cash flow rather than revenue, warning that a $5M break-even company can be worth less than a profitable $1M one [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:01:08]. Campbell puts it bluntly: cash flow services debt and pays the owner [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:01:34]. Quiet Light Brokerage repeats the formula for online sellers, stating that a business's value is based on a multiple of its earnings and that buyers treat SDE as their baseline for estimating return on investment [R4jvbLHhCBg @ 00:00:26]. Ryan C. Winter reduces it to earnings times multiple, $300K at 3x for roughly $900K [tPnDBaB9oPU @ 00:01:02], and warns operators off revenue rules of thumb entirely [tPnDBaB9oPU @ 00:03:58]. Campbell backs that warning with a scar: a listing priced at 3x revenue, $15M on $5M of sales and roughly 10x cash flow, never sold [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:09:04]. Price conversations therefore open on documented profit, never on top-line volume, years in business, debts the seller owes or the seller's retirement number.

Practitioners also agree on which earnings number to multiply, and the switch turns on whether the buyer is buying a job or a managed company. Keira Hamilton notes that SDE and EBITDA both add back interest, taxes, depreciation, amortization, one-time items and discretionary spending, while SDE alone also adds back owner salary [1dJeO4qEAhU @ 00:00:20]. Peter Nola labels SDE 'return to a working owner,' its New Zealand name [RoGz5NZF96I @ 00:00:38], and calls EBITDA 'managed profit' calculated after owner pay [RoGz5NZF96I @ 00:01:39], the standard in M&A for medium, large and capital-intensive firms [RoGz5NZF96I @ 00:03:16]. David C Barnett draws the line near $500K: SDE for owner-operated firms below it at about 2-2.2x and lower for service firms, EBITDA above it [Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:03:34], and EBIT or EBITDA minus capex for capital-intensive operators like trucking [Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:04:46]. Brett Cenkus places the salary add-back mainly around $1-2M deals, where buyers 'buy themselves a job,' while at roughly $20M management is retained and no salary comes back [y4u_MuL4xhw @ 00:05:11]. The size cutoff floats from adviser to adviser, but the logic holds: once a paid manager runs the business, the owner's paycheck stops counting as discretionary earnings and the buyer prices a managed cash stream.

On what moves the multiple, the risk lists line up almost item for item. Campbell names owner dependence, customer concentration around 30-40%, recurring revenue, trend, clean books, industry and size, and warns that 'the more a business depends on the owner at listing time, the more it will depend on the owner at closing time' [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:06:46]. Winter's list is nearly identical, flagging a single client at 50% of revenue as a red flag alongside owner dependence, trend, clean books and team [tPnDBaB9oPU @ 00:02:49]. Arthur Petropoulos explains why bigger companies earn bigger multiples: less key-person risk and a broader buyer pool, a dynamic labeled 'EBITDA expansion' that drives roll-ups, summed up as 'same work, different deals' [brFD1fFAYhQ @ 00:01:12]. On the SaaS side, David Newell of Quiet Light, who has sold 75-plus businesses including Drip, names key-man risk as mistake number one: document the code, hand it to a trusted developer or CTO, and step out quickly, the way Rob Walling brought in Derek as CTO and left the code after about six months [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:04:39]. Every one of these levers is about transferability. A buyer pays up for earnings that survive the seller walking out the door, and discounts every dollar that leaves with the founder.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The SDE build follows a repeatable sequence. Quiet Light's method strips non-cash expenses like amortization and depreciation plus taxes and interest, then owner benefits such as salary and home office, 'because how much you pay yourself is entirely up to you,' then true one-time expenses like building an app, then situational adjustments [R4jvbLHhCBg @ 00:01:14]. Nate Lind starts at the top line: gross sales minus chargebacks and refunds, COGS, SG&A and non-operating income such as PPP or EIDL money and lawsuit settlements [yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:01:39]. Lind then allows depreciation, interest and amortization, one-time website retrofits, the 2021 freight-cost delta and recruiter fees as add-backs [yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:04:01]. Tyler Jeffcoat of Seller Accountant runs trailing-twelve-month SDE off an accrual-basis P&L, walking $1M in sales, $340K gross profit and $100K operating profit to $185K of SDE [jkHzL8ya984 @ 00:06:26]. Jeffcoat's filter: unused rent, owner salary and a VA come back; core tools like a Skubana ERP and core contractors stay in, because 'you win every ad back battle that you don't have to have' [jkHzL8ya984 @ 00:05:06]. Brent Freeman of the CBB Group shows the stack on a real P&L: $924K plus $15K interest, $40K depreciation and $210K owner comp yields $1.189M of SDE [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:04:53].

With normalized earnings locked in, the multiple grid is remarkably well mapped. Campbell runs Main Street SDE at 2-3.5x off comps and industry datasets, stacking $150K net, $100K owner pay and $50K add-backs into $300K of SDE that lands near $825K at about 2.75x, while nudging the multiple to 3.25x adds $150K [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:05:06]. Keira Hamilton quotes a typical 3-5x, with $500K of SDE at 4x producing $2M [1dJeO4qEAhU @ 00:01:28]. Petropoulos, whose Hillview Partners serves $1M-$20M EBITDA companies, maps the institutional ladder: $500K-$1M of EBITDA at 3-5x, $1-3M revised up to 5-9x, $3-5M at 6-9x with many $3M companies trading at 7-8x, $5-10M at 6-10x, and above $10M at 12x, with 15x and 20x printed in frothy markets [D58oCe_7BBM @ 00:04:07]. The arbitrage math explains PE appetite: buy ten $1M-EBITDA companies at 6x for $60M, then sell the combined $10M of EBITDA at 10x for $100M [D58oCe_7BBM @ 00:08:00]. Newell values sub-$1M-ARR SaaS on SDE at 3-5x, so a $500K-ARR product throwing off $200K of profit prices at $600K-$1M [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:10:22]. With the median near 4x [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:13:41], every $50K of add-backs is worth $200K of price, which is why the add-back fight matters so much [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:12:36].

The financing desk then decides whether the price survives. Deal Street's financing breakdown sets SBA 7(a) loans at up to $5M covering as much as 90% of goodwill, a buyer injection of at least 10% that cannot be borrowed [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:02:23], a 1.25 minimum DSCR as of October 1, 2026, no projections counted toward DSCR, and an independent QoE on deals of $3M-plus [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:03:08]. Campbell defines DSCR as cash flow plus owner salary divided by annual debt service, warning that if the price is so high that cash flow can't comfortably support the debt, the deal won't get financed [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:12:46]. Freeman's live structure: $3M price, 15% or $450K down, a $2.55M SBA loan over 10 years at 8.5% for $31,616 a month, producing 2.25:1 coverage with $150K of owner comp and 1.92:1 on a modified basis that charges a 20% return on the down payment, $7,500 a month [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:12:28]. Seller notes fill the gap at 10-20% of price over 3-7 years, often amortized over 10-plus years with a 3-5 year balloon [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:05:13]; a note funding the buyer's down payment sits on full standby for the SBA loan's life [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:06:31] and can cover at most half that injection [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:07:20].

callout.title: Add-back and structure moves the brokers actually run
callout.body: Small, documented adjustments compound through the multiple, and deal structure decides what the seller actually banks.
items: Apply a confirmed hosting cut retroactively: dropping from $8K to $4K a month credits $4K x 10 months, or $40K, to trailing earnings, and a one-time $10-15K website overhaul can be added back [Quiet Light Brokerage — oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:48:11].

Pull PPP or EIDL money and lawsuit settlements out as non-operating income, then add back recruiter fees and the 2021 freight-cost delta as one-time items [Nate Lind - Business Broker and Beyond — yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:01:39].

Shop lenders to the add-back schedule: SBA lenders vary in whether owner salary and depreciation come back in full, in part or not at all, so match the lender to the add-backs [Keira Hamilton — 1dJeO4qEAhU @ 00:02:40].
Use the seller-note trick of the trade: amortize over 10-plus years with a balloon at year 3-5 that usually gets refinanced [Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A — a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:05:13].

sop_steps.title: Rebuild trailing earnings
sop_steps.action: Reconstruct trailing-twelve-month earnings on an accrual-basis P&L before touching add-backs.
sop_steps.detail: Start from gross sales, subtract chargebacks, refunds, COGS and SG&A, and strip non-operating income such as PPP/EIDL money and lawsuit settlements [Nate Lind - Business Broker and Beyond — yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:01:39]; run the result on TTM accrual books [Seller Accountant — jkHzL8ya984 @ 00:06:26].

sop_steps.title: Layer defensible add-backs
sop_steps.action: Add back non-cash items, owner benefits, true one-time spend and situational adjustments only where documented.
sop_steps.detail: Follow the four-step SDE sequence of non-cash items, owner benefits, one-time expenses and situational adjustments [Quiet Light Brokerage — R4jvbLHhCBg @ 00:01:14]; expect lenders to reject meals, travel, car and entertainment and accept medical insurance only if documented [Brent Freeman  - The CBB Group — pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:05:58].

sop_steps.title: Pick the earnings measure and multiple band
sop_steps.action: Choose SDE, EBITDA or EBITDA minus capex by size and capital intensity, then place the business in its band.
sop_steps.detail: Use SDE below roughly $500K and EBITDA above it, with EBITDA minus capex for trucking-type firms [David C Barnett Small Business and Deal Making SMB — Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:03:34]; place EBITDA companies on the 3-5x to 12x size ladder [Arthur Petropoulos — D58oCe_7BBM @ 00:04:07].

sop_steps.title: Stress-test price against the lender
sop_steps.action: Run DSCR on the proposed SBA structure before the number goes to market.
sop_steps.detail: Compute DSCR as cash flow plus owner salary over annual debt service against the 1.25 minimum [Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A — ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:11:50]; model the full structure the way Freeman did, a $3M price at 2.25:1 standard and 1.92:1 modified coverage [Brent Freeman  - The CBB Group — pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:12:28].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The add-back fight is where brokers split hardest, and the split moves real dollars. Shep Campbell at Deal Street adds back W-2 owner salary and payroll taxes plus life insurance and family members' phones, vehicles and health plans, yet refuses to add back the owner's personal vehicle, phone or health insurance [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:02:25]. Ryan C. Winter runs the opposite playbook: salary, interest, taxes, depreciation, one-time items and the personal vehicle, phone and travel all go back in, and Winter reports SDE often lands 40 to 50 percent above tax-return profit [tPnDBaB9oPU @ 00:01:56]. Brent Freeman of the CBB Group says that inflated number dies at the bank, because lenders treat tax returns as the source of truth and refuse meals, travel, car and entertainment add-backs, accepting medical insurance only when documented [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:05:58]. Nate Lind splits the difference: travel, meals, personal auto and phone are generally accepted, but SBA lenders rule on them case by case [yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:03:14]. The operator read: the aggressive schedule wins the listing conversation, the conservative schedule wins the financing conversation, so build both versions before quoting a seller any number at all.

Practitioners also disagree on where SDE stops and EBITDA starts, and on which multiple belongs to each. David C Barnett uses SDE for owner-operated firms under roughly $500K at about 2 to 2.2 times, lower for service firms, switches to EBITDA above $500K, and moves capital-intensive operators like trucking to EBIT or EBITDA minus capex [Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:03:34]. Brent Freeman puts the switch at about $1M and above, noting the EBITDA multiple is always higher [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:11:00]. Brett Cenkus ties the owner-salary add-back to the $1 to 2M band, where buyers buy themselves a job, and drops it near $20M because management stays on [y4u_MuL4xhw @ 00:05:11]. SaaS breaks the pattern entirely: David Newell at Quiet Light values sub-$1M ARR deals on SDE, but over $1M ARR private equity and strategic buyers price on revenue and will accept thin EBITDA if the founder is out of the code, churn stays under 4 percent a month, and growth runs 30 to 50 percent a year [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:08:13]. Pick the earnings metric first, because it decides which multiple band a seller is even allowed to argue for, and which buyer pool will show up to the table.

Financing thresholds and pre-sale earnings tuning are the third fault line. Deal Street states the SBA 7(a) minimum DSCR moved from 1.2 to 1.25, with projections no longer allowed toward the ratio [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:03:35]. Brent Freeman says lenders want at least 1.5 in this interest rate environment, and runs a modified DSCR that credits the buyer a 20 percent return on the down payment, $7,500 a month, which drags a 2.25:1 deal down to 1.92:1 [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:12:28]. On juicing the trailing twelve months, the 2025 Quiet Light panel split live: Tom is very anti, while John Hanstock says it depends, arguing that switching AWS to reserved pricing and showing three months of savings can justify applying them across the trailing 12 months [In6A5W0WFdY @ 00:34:26]. David Newell goes further, applying a hosting cut from $8K to $4K a month retroactively, $4K times 10 months, for a $40K adjustment, and treating a one-time $10 to 15K website overhaul as an add-back [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:48:11]. The split playbook: underwrite to the 1.5 cushion and clean books when the deal needs bank money, and save retroactive savings adjustments for the buyer who can actually pay for them without a lender's sign-off.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures start at the listing price. Shep Campbell at Deal Street once listed a business at 3 times revenue, $15M on $5M of revenue, roughly 10 times cash flow, and it never sold; the same broker names selling into a downturn as mistake number two and warns that add-back-everything schedules raise red flags with buyers [ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:09:04]. Ryan C. Winter bans revenue rules of thumb outright and treats one client at 50 percent of revenue as a red flag that drags the multiple down [tPnDBaB9oPU @ 00:03:58]. Aswath Damodaran shows why cheap-looking multiples trap buyers: the private equity rule that under 6 times EBITDA is cheap would have flagged about 10,000 of roughly 40,000 global companies in 2013 and half of all companies in 2009, so the fix is the 20th percentile or first quartile recalculated each year [xI-KTlxfNDU @ 00:04:12]. Damodaran's Ryder System case, at 2.91 times, looked cheap but carried the oldest fleet in the sector and would need debt to replace it [xI-KTlxfNDU @ 00:11:07]. The economics check is mismatch-hunting: a low multiple sitting on old assets, high taxes or heavy reinvestment needs is usually priced correctly, not a bargain waiting for a sharp buyer.

The second cluster of losses happens between handshake and funding. Brent Freeman warns that a broker ends up selling the transaction three times, to the buyer, the lender and the appraiser, and that lenders underwrite off tax returns, so add-backs that cannot survive that review die at the bank; Freeman's protection is a clawback through seller-note forgiveness if add-backs prove false [pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:07:41]. Deal Street adds the hard SBA mechanics: a seller note funding the buyer's down payment goes on full standby, with no payments or interest for the life of the SBA loan, and the SBA will not finance earnouts at all [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:06:31]. Keira Hamilton reports SBA lenders vary on whether owner salary and depreciation get added back in full, in part or not at all, so the lender has to match the add-back schedule [1dJeO4qEAhU @ 00:02:40]. Deal Street's two-offer comparison is the economics check: Offer A at $1.2M cash, a $500K note and a $500K earnout loses to Offer B at $1.7M cash and a $200K note, which puts $500K more in the seller's pocket on day one [a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:13:04]. Price the structure, not the headline.

SaaS and concentration traps destroy value quietly. David Newell at Quiet Light ranks key-man risk as mistake number one, calls lifetime plans suicidal after one surfaced within 24 hours of due diligence, and lists heavy discounting and halting development for more than 3 to 6 months as value destroyers; the timing fix is to avoid selling exhausted or mid-rebuild and aim for about six months after a major release [oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:39:54]. On the 2025 Quiet Light panel, Tom walked away from a custom-data contract worth about half a team member's salary because one-off revenue is not worth anything to buyers, and flags COGS at 20 percent as a possible misclassification signal against a target near 5 percent [In6A5W0WFdY @ 00:17:52]. David C Barnett's concentration case, 60 percent of revenue from four clients, gets handled with seller notes subject to offset rather than a blunt price cut [Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:13:35]. Brett Cenkus goes harder: a business living on two customers may be unsellable or sold only at a discount [y4u_MuL4xhw @ 00:10:18]. Clean these up before listing, because diligence finds them anyway.

callout.title: Four checks before a number goes in front of a seller or buyer
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, a dead listing or a diligence blowup the practitioners reported. Clear all four before quoting price or signing a structure.
items: Refuse to list on a revenue multiple; a 3 times revenue listing at roughly 10 times cash flow never sold [Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A — ggUaT-lHV0A @ 00:09:04].

Run DSCR at the lender's current floor, at least 1.5 in this rate environment, and again with a 20 percent down-payment return before listing [Brent Freeman  - The CBB Group — pzqh4R8Hppk @ 00:12:28].
Match the SBA lender to the add-back schedule, since lenders differ on owner salary and depreciation in full, in part or not at all [Keira Hamilton — 1dJeO4qEAhU @ 00:02:40].
Kill lifetime plans, heavy discounting and founder dependence in the code before diligence opens, because they surface within 24 hours [Quiet Light Brokerage — oJsHo5vaDus @ 00:39:54].

chapters.pull_quote: "Do not fall in love with the headline price." Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A (a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:15:02).
action_checklist: Build SDE from trailing-twelve-month figures on an accrual-basis P&L, not cash-basis books [Seller Accountant — jkHzL8ya984 @ 00:06:26].
Strip non-operating income such as PPP and EIDL money and lawsuit settlements before adding anything back [Nate Lind - Business Broker and Beyond — yaZZzBKh86I @ 00:01:39].
Pull comparables matched on industry, geography and revenue range from bizbuysell.com, then add real estate and equipment and subtract assumed liabilities [Brett Cenkus — y4u_MuL4xhw @ 00:06:24].
Cross-check the SDE multiple against EBITDA net of a fair wage: $150K SDE at 2 times can equal 5 to 6 times EBITDA [David C Barnett Small Business and Deal Making SMB — Va5USDqv3-A @ 00:09:56].

Structure seller notes at 10 to 20 percent of price, amortized over 10-plus years with a 3 to 5 year balloon, backed by credit check, personal guarantee and security interest [Deal Street - Small to Lower Middle Market M&A — a5Z--B3Uhrg @ 00:05:13].
Map the EBITDA band to its buyer pool and multiple, $1 to 3M at 5 to 9 times, and pitch PE platforms and search funds accordingly [Arthur Petropoulos — D58oCe_7BBM @ 00:04:36].

chapters.question_prompt: What market-specific considerations distinguish online-business purchases, telecom lease transactions, data-center land selection, and transferable tax-credit purchases?
chapters.title: Specialist Markets: Digital Businesses, Infrastructure, and Tax Credits
chapters.subtitle: Online-business broker and marketplace reviews, SaaS sourcing and website communication, cell-tower lease buyouts and easements, powered-land site selection, and Section 6418 credit transfers
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners in four specialist lanes converge on one rule: price the paper, not the pitch. Digital operators favor specialist brokers like Quiet Light, which claims to reject 90% of applicants and charges 10% of the first $1 million, over open marketplaces like Flippa, where unserious buyers and scammers roam. FE International closes 94% of listings but publishes no upfront pricing and bills buyers up to $1,000. Tower Genius pegs cell tower buyouts at 16 to 18 times annual rent depending on a right of first refusal, while SiteBid favors perpetual easements for bigger checks and 1031 treatment. Data center teams start with a utility load ramp, and Andrew Dubinsky warns 6418 credit buyers carry the IRS risk. Disagreements center on Quiet Light: Francis Walsh is a huge fan, while Colin Matcha found its team distant and cold.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the digital-business side, the loudest agreement is that specialization beats generalists once a deal gets serious. Chris, a long-time buyer who has worked with franchise and independent brokers, says the single lesson they learned without doubt is to go with a specialized broker rather than one that lists pizza shops, liquor stores, and auto service in the same book [NSNpSgvzAyA @ 00:00:05]. Francis Walsh of The Digital Merchant lands in the same place, saying they are a big fan of specialization and steering non-SaaS sellers away from Acquire.com because it is built around SaaS startup assets [yd4nlCQanq4 @ 00:09:17]. The market splits into three operating models. Full-service brokers such as FE International and Quiet Light find buyers for you, gate access, and broker the deal; open platforms such as Flippa let buyers and sellers deal directly with little vetting; and acquirers such as Onfolio buy the business outright, but only above $500,000 a year in profit [yd4nlCQanq4 @ 00:10:32]. Colin Matcha, an SEO operator of seven years who brokers digital assets for clients, frames the buy side the same way: you will end up shopping both brokerages and marketplaces, but only the brokerage model gives you a dedicated broker, a prospectus, and a gatekeeper between you and the seller [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:03:04].

The second consensus point: curation is the product, and the broker works for the seller. Colin Matcha reports Quiet Light claims to reject 90% of the sellers who want to list, which is why they rate its listings the highest quality in the space [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:09:58]. Business Solution describes Empire Flippers only accepting established businesses clearing roughly $1,500 to $2,000 a month in net profit over the trailing 12 months, with every listing reviewed before it goes live [zcYOmZ8cAGE @ 00:00:55]. Chris adds that Quiet Light pre-vets its buyer list too, running NDAs and proof of funds before anyone sees confidential data, and that the buyer pool is already networked: individual tech investors, search fund operators, family offices, and smaller private equity groups [NSNpSgvzAyA @ 00:08:27]. The flip side, which Colin Matcha hammers on both reviews, is that these firms represent the seller and are paid a percentage of the sale price, so every extra dollar of price is extra commission for them; at FE International that cut is 15%, and the brokers 'are not really on your side' when you negotiate [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:14:04]. Operators who internalize that alignment treat the broker as the seller's agent, use them for information flow, and run their own diligence regardless of how curated the feed looks.

In the hard-asset and tax-credit lanes the consensus is the same instinct applied to different paper: the document behind the asset is what gets priced. On cell towers, Mike Travis of Nexus Towers says property owners misread the deal: a tower easement sells only the specific area the tower uses, not the building or rooftop, and works like a deed that lets the buyer securitize that little section while the owner keeps everything else [YjzN5Uo5yf8 @ 00:00:14]. On data centers, Data Center Build Academy says power is factor number one 'and it's not close', so the first call goes to the utility rather than a real estate broker [8UjhKryCNbQ @ 00:00:44], and Reed Smith calls 'powered land' a marketing term because a utility letter of intent is very different from a signed agreement [HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:00:30]. On transferable tax credits, Andrew Dubinsky stresses that a Section 6418 credit is 'just an idea' until the project is placed in service and the IRS issues a registration number, and even then the number is a claim check that does not confer validity on the credit [h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:08:50]. Every one of these practitioners prices the paper, not the pitch.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The fee math is where the platforms separate. Colin Matcha lays out Quiet Light's ladder: 10% of the first $1 million, so a $500,000 deal pays $50,000, and a $1.5 million deal pays $145,000 once the second million drops to 9%; they note FE International and Empire Flippers both charge 15% [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:08:09]. Business Solution breaks down Empire Flippers' blended structure: a $7,000 minimum, 15% on the portion up to roughly $700,000, 8% between $700,000 and $5 million, and 2.5% above that, with nothing paid upfront to list [zcYOmZ8cAGE @ 00:01:36]. Flippa runs the opposite model, charging listing fees starting around $29 to $49 plus tiered success fees up to about 10%, higher if you buy its partner broker service, while Investors Club charges sellers nothing and monetizes buyer memberships instead [zcYOmZ8cAGE @ 00:04:38]. On the buy side, Colin Matcha flags FE International as the one brokerage charging buyers a fee, capped at $1,000, plus escrow.com costs including a $75 domain holding fee; pay by wire transfer for the smallest fee and skip credit cards because the points will not cover the difference [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:14:38]. Model these fees before listing, because Business Solution notes sellers bake commissions into asking prices.

On the buy side, Colin Matcha's workflow at FE International is concrete. Sign the NDA once, request the prospectus, and expect it within one to two business days; the PDF carries the P&L, analytics traffic, growth strategies, and seller Q&A [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:07:21]. Read the asterisk: listing figures are often annualized off the last three months, which Colin Matcha calls really short when six months is the usual floor. FE International generally will not hand over Google Analytics or Search Console access, so ask for specifics instead: the last 30 days versus the previous 30, year-on-year traffic, and the top 25 pages by traffic [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:09:08]. When a broker stalls, a non-binding letter of intent signals seriousness and tends to unlock more data and faster replies. At Quiet Light the NDA unlocks a business summary, a seller interview in video and audio, and a monthly P&L, and listings flag whether lenders are pre-approved or the deal is SBA eligible [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:04:49]. Both firms keep the buyer off the negotiating table: offers go through the broker by email, and Quiet Light accepts all-cash offers at listing price by default [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:05:41]. Price itself is a multiple of profit, which FE International quotes in years.

Tower and credit deals have their own street math. Tower Genius says buyout calculators do not exist, but gives a rule of thumb: with a right of first refusal in the lease, offers land around 16 to 17 times annual rent; without one, 17 to 18 times, and a second opinion can surface money left on the table [V2LGinURueI @ 00:01:03]. SiteBid Infrastructure ranks easement scopes: specific easements match the leased footprint and are least preferred because they block new tenants, general easements over a full rooftop draw the highest valuations and can carry a 50/50 revenue share, and expanded easements add roughly 500 square feet [fLebm5BppxY @ 00:01:04]. For data centers, Reed Smith says diligence starts with a load ramp from the utility stating megawatts and timing, such as one gigawatt in five years, which is valuable but not now [HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:01:09]. Andrew Dubinsky's 6418 sequence is: place the project in service, register on the IRS energy credit portal, wait two weeks to two months for the registration number, sign the transfer agreement, then the buyer claims the credit on Form 3800 with that number while the seller reports the transfer [h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:07:16].
