callout.title: Deal-flow and structuring edges practitioners actually use
callout.body: Four moves the speakers run to get better deal flow, better information, and cleaner closings than the default listing process gives them.
items: Sign up for the FE International newsletter and tell them the exact SaaS business type and budget you want, so the broker pushes matching deals to you and you only review what fits [Jaryd Krause - Buying Online Businesses — XbluQ7u-9nc @ 00:01:23].

Hunt SaaS off-market: join SaaS Facebook groups and forums and announce you are buying, because some owners who never considered selling will say yes once asked [Jaryd Krause - Buying Online Businesses — XbluQ7u-9nc @ 00:03:20].

On loosely run brokerages, a stray phone number or data point in the teaser can let you identify the business before signing anything; Chris says Quiet Light locks this down with strict confidentiality steps [The Digital Merchant — NSNpSgvzAyA @ 00:07:31].

If a landowner's lender objects to an easement on title, Nexus Towers structures the sale as a Master Lease so it records as a lease and no easement shows on the property [Nexus Towers — YjzN5Uo5yf8 @ 00:01:35].

sop_steps.title: Match the venue to deal size and asset type
sop_steps.action: Route sub-$150,000 deals to Flippa or smaller marketplaces, high-end e-commerce and FBA to Quiet Light, and profitable SaaS to FE International.
sop_steps.detail: Colin Matcha says Quiet Light is not great for acquisitions under $150,000 and points smaller buyers to Empire Flippers, Flippa, or smaller marketplaces, while rating FE International the best profitable-SaaS brokerage across all levels [Colin Matcha — l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:11:42].

sop_steps.title: Get the paper under NDA
sop_steps.action: Put an NDA on file, pull the prospectus or business summary, and log the seller interview and monthly P&L.
sop_steps.detail: At FE International the prospectus usually arrives within one to two business days once the NDA is on file, carrying the P&L, analytics traffic, growth strategies, and seller Q&A [Colin Matcha — r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:07:21].

sop_steps.title: Pressure-test the numbers
sop_steps.action: De-annualize three-month figures and request targeted traffic pulls instead of waiting for analytics access.
sop_steps.detail: Ask for the last 30 days versus the previous 30, year-on-year traffic, and the top 25 pages by traffic, and use a non-binding LOI to unlock more data and faster responses [Colin Matcha — r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:09:08].

sop_steps.title: Close through APA, escrow, and a migration channel
sop_steps.action: Sign the asset purchase agreement, fund escrow by wire, and run a dedicated handover channel for accounts and hosting.
sop_steps.detail: Colin Matcha's most recent FE International APA ran 11 pages, escrow.com handled the domain, and in both of their deals FE International set up a dedicated Skype channel to migrate hosting, affiliate, and social accounts [Colin Matcha — r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:11:54].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the digital-business lane is Quiet Light versus FE International, and practitioners who have worked both sides do not land in the same place. Francis Walsh of The Digital Merchant says Quiet Light gets the first call at the mid-market level, because FEI hides its pricing, serves the same revenue band, and does not cater to any segment better than its competitors [yd4nlCQanq4 @ 00:13:55]. Chris, shopping for online businesses from the buy side, backs that read: every Quiet Light advisor has started, bought, or sold an online business, a whole-org-chart model Chris never saw in years of dealing with franchise and independent brokers [NSNpSgvzAyA @ 00:03:25]. Colin Matcha pushes back on the relationship side, reporting that the Quiet Light team came across as distant and cold at a happy hour [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:01:45]. Matcha credits FEI with in-person events and email follow-up no other online broker comes close to, and routes deals by asset class: profitable SaaS at any size goes to FEI, called probably the best profitable SaaS brokerage across all levels, while unprofitable SaaS goes to MicroAcquire [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:18:44]. The operator move is picking the house by asset class and deal size, not by brand reputation.

Curated versus open marketplace is the second fault line. Business Solution names Empire Flippers its top pick for a curated deal flow, but The Digital Merchant would still send a mid-market seller to Quiet Light over Empire, arguing the consultants carry better expertise, the vetting is less painful, and the value for money is stronger [yd4nlCQanq4 @ 00:11:52]. On Flippa the two channels agree on the facts and split on the verdict. The Digital Merchant says four- and five-figure sellers can do good business there, but anything more serious drowns in time-wasters, unserious buyers, and even scammers because buyer vetting is thin [yd4nlCQanq4 @ 00:08:33]. Business Solution frames the same openness as an edge: lots of deal flow, smaller listings bigger brokers ignore, and a good fit for buyers who like hunting deals and are happy to verify everything themselves [zcYOmZ8cAGE @ 00:05:43]. A third playbook flips the fee model entirely. Investors Club charges sellers no listing or success fee, so sellers keep 100% of proceeds, and monetizes through buyer memberships instead, backed by an exclusivity agreement that keeps the listing from being blasted everywhere [zcYOmZ8cAGE @ 00:07:04]. Choose the venue by whether you are paying with commission, membership dues, or your own diligence hours.

In cell tower deals the split is structure: keep the land clean or take the bigger check. SiteBid Infrastructure lays out the master lease as the simpler path, where a new lease is written with fresh terms and the current tenant becomes a sublease, keeping property rights intact but usually paying less because the buyer's control is limited [EsfznycDU6I @ 00:00:44]. The perpetual easement, often 99 years, pays a bigger upfront number, hands lease management to the buyer, and opens the door to a 1031 exchange into other real estate [EsfznycDU6I @ 00:01:30]. Mike Travis of Nexus Towers works the opposite angle for owners who hate the word easement: when a lender would give an owner a hard time over an easement shown on the property, Nexus has structured the same deal as a master lease so it records as a lease and never shows as an easement [YjzN5Uo5yf8 @ 00:01:35]. Pricing philosophy splits too. Tower Genius says no buyout calculator exists and every site is priced on location, tenant, and buyer appetite, then still gives a rule of thumb: annual rent times 16 or 17 with a right of first refusal in the lease, 17 or 18 without one [V2LGinURueI @ 00:01:03]. Treat that multiple as an opening anchor, not a ceiling.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first buyer-side trap is reading broker numbers at face value. Colin Matcha flags that FE International listing figures carry an asterisk: revenue and profit are annualized off the last three months, meaning those months multiplied by four, and Matcha calls three months really short when six is the usual floor [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:06:30]. On Quiet Light, the stale-data problem shows up differently: listings that sit longer than a month can carry a prospectus still showing August numbers in October, even though September is fully closed [l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:10:33]. The second trap is forgetting who the broker works for. Matcha is blunt that brokers represent the seller and earn a cut of the sale price, 15% at FEI, so they are incentivized to sell for as much as possible and are not really on your side when you negotiate [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:14:20]. Then the fees leak at closing. FEI is the only brokerage Matcha knows that charges buyers a fee, capped at $1,000, and escrow.com adds a $75 domain holding fee plus a percentage fee by transaction size, with the smallest fees near 0.89 on a wire transfer; Matcha warns that credit card points will not make up the difference [r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:14:57].

Infrastructure buyers get burned by power promises. Data Center Build Academy opens with the nightmare: a company buys two hundred acres of flat, fairly priced land, calls the utility, and learns the needed power will not be available for six years, a scenario described as real and happening across the industry right now [8UjhKryCNbQ @ 00:00:00]. Reed Smith LLP treats the phrase itself as the trap, calling powered land a marketing term because power commitments come in very different forms, and a letter of intent is very different from a signed agreement; that has to be pinned down early, before clients burn time, money, and resources chasing a site with no contracted power [HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:00:30]. The Reed Smith fix is contractual: off ramps and flexibility to terminate if power is not or cannot be contractually committed in the client's timeframe, plus walk-away or renegotiation rights if a moratorium blocks the build [HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:02:17]. Zoning is the second killer. In the Academy's three-site case, Site C had power in two years but strong local opposition to rezoning, and the team passed because a rezoning delay can cost more than the land itself, while Site A's six-year power timeline made it almost worthless for now [8UjhKryCNbQ @ 00:04:59].

Tax credit buyers carry the downside after the wire. Andrew Dubinsky is explicit that once a 6418 credit is transferred, the buyer is liable for anything the IRS objects to and has to collect from the seller; Dubinsky pegs an IRS invalidation at about a one in 20,000 chance, but the buyer is effectively on the hook for the money anyway [h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:05:27]. The pitch trap is the registration number. Dubinsky warns that a seller saying the IRS registered the credits means nothing, because the number is a tracking number, a claim check that confers no validity or blessing [h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:08:50]. Supply is also less ready than it looks: most credits are not ready to transact when they hit the market, either too early, still under construction, or, on smaller credits, short on information for a comprehensive transaction, much like a house that needs work before listing [Z0ATgOouiIM @ 00:03:08]. On the tower side, the cost of going alone is money left behind. Tower Genius says every site must be looked at individually and a second opinion pays because owners can leave a little or a heck of a lot of money on the table against big wireless [V2LGinURueI @ 00:01:21].

callout.title: Four Hard Stops Before You Sign
callout.body: Each stop comes straight from losses, stalls, and traps practitioners reported across digital M&A, powered land, transferable tax credits, and cell tower buyouts. Clear all four before money moves.
items: Do not underwrite a digital asset off three months of annualized numbers; demand six months and targeted traffic pulls [Colin Matcha — r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:06:30].
Do not pay a powered-land premium without a signed power agreement, a dated load ramp, and an off ramp if power or a moratorium blocks the build [Reed Smith LLP — HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:02:17].
Do not accept an IRS registration number as proof a tax credit is valid, because the buyer is on the hook after transfer [Andrew Dubinsky — h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:08:50].
Do not sign a tower buyout offer without benchmarking it against the 16 to 18 times annual rent range and getting a second opinion [Tower Genius — V2LGinURueI @ 00:01:03].

chapters.pull_quote: Powered land is the premium. That is what's driving the cost. So if the power is not there, it's not actually committed, now we maybe need to reconsider. — Reed Smith LLP (HXjpQWcZ6F8 @ 00:01:31)
action_checklist: Line up broker fee schedules side by side before engaging; Quiet Light takes 10% of the first million while FEI and Empire Flippers charge 15% [Colin Matcha — l-9E6P1CSEc @ 00:07:53].
Tell FE International and other brokers exactly what SaaS model and budget you want so matching deals land in front of you first [Jaryd Krause - Buying Online Businesses — XbluQ7u-9nc @ 00:01:23].
Fund escrow.com by wire transfer to hit the lowest fee tier, and skip credit cards because the points will not cover the difference [Colin Matcha — r4fmjknWB7o @ 00:14:57].
Make the first data center site call to the utility and get how many megawatts can be delivered, and when, in writing [Data Center Build Academy — 8UjhKryCNbQ @ 00:00:59].

Confirm each tax credit carries its own IRS registration number, with separate numbers for hybrid solar-plus-battery systems, before signing the transfer agreement [Andrew Dubinsky — h0qEAIoQ4Jo @ 00:08:34].
If a lender objects to an easement shown on the property, structure the tower sale as a master lease so it records as a lease [Nexus Towers — YjzN5Uo5yf8 @ 00:01:35].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I present an acquisition opportunity, evaluate offers beyond headline price, and identify diligence and documentation problems that can prevent closing?
chapters.title: From Deal Presentation to Diligence and Closing Certainty
chapters.subtitle: Business-buying steps, Main Street legal practices and market terms, CIM creation and AI generation, offer risk, online-business sale lessons, paperwork failures, private-market diligence, freight-broker fraud, and Axial deal experience
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Main Street brokerage, SMB deal law, lower middle market private equity and the Axial platform agree that closing certainty is built before the buyer arrives. That means tax returns that tie to P&Ls, receipts for every add-back, honest CIMs and fast responses. Speed is treated as leverage: the target close is 3 to 6 months, and fatigue sets in at 4 to 6 months. Trust breaks the moment a buyer discovers what the seller hid. The street mechanics are specific: 60-to-90-day binding exclusivity, SBA debt under $5M, and an $800K/$100K/$100K stack with a subordinated seller note that carries set-off rights instead of escrow. Up market, indemnity caps run 10 to 20 percent, and R&W insurance costs 25 to 50 bps once deals pass $20M to $50M. Disagreements center on deposits, 100% seller financing, AI-drafted documents and how hard to push off-market terms.

key_metrics.context: Peter Lehrman's count of lower middle market deals attempted on Axial each year that close, with either an Axial or a non-Axial buyer.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Certainty of Close Is Built Before the Buyer Arrives
paragraphs: Across the sell side and the buy side, operators converge on one rule: deals are won or lost on whether the numbers survive verification. Charles Weatherly names the three standard deal killers. They are unverifiable add-backs, financials that do not tie to tax returns, and owner dependence. Problems a buyer discovers get repriced in the buyer's favor, or the buyer walks, and relistings rarely come back at the same price [55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:00:01]. Mark Sims says valuation "begins and ends" with the financials and what both sides can agree on [uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:05:01]. Host Matt Uhler adds that buyers often deduct more than the actual fix would cost, and has watched $300,000 bookkeeper mistakes surface. Quiet Light's $1.7M exit shows the payoff of the same discipline. The business was an educational product roughly 8 to 9 years old, netting $450,000, and its tax returns matched its P&Ls. That made it "SBA pre-qualified" against an estimated 3.5x multiple [ow7ewDogN14 @ 00:08:02]. The Carter Morse seller started "from zero." Next time, the seller would prepare more, build out the management team, and get finances "buttoned down" before engaging a bank [a71tQJb9UFE @ 00:01:08]. The baseline is the same in every camp: reconcile first, go to market second.

Price alone does not win the mandate; certainty of close does. The Carter Morse seller says that after price, the deciding criterion was certainty of close, because anyone can write a good offer. The seller picked a partner who could add expertise and actually get the deal done [a71tQJb9UFE @ 00:00:02]. Quiet Light's advisor immediately rejects "full price" LOIs that are 100% seller financed over a 10-year payout at a meager rate, such as $19,000 a month. The reason is that "there is a transfer of risk that has to happen in the deals that we do," and these structures leave the seller holding the risk without the money [_t4Q9Q7VTtQ @ 00:01:13]. Cash buyers, by contrast, are "the bell of the ball." Jake Parsley reaches the same conclusion from the buyer's counsel seat. Parsley treats 100% seller-financed deals as a warning sign, but accepts a seller note sized as one slice of the capital stack and subordinated to the SBA loan [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:26:32]. Peter Lehrman adds the reputational layer: missing reputation between counterparties breaks deals. A single closed deal cancels a rival's "better-capitalized" advantage, so references should be offered up front rather than hidden [8mBk6b5QR5I @ 00:12:08].

Every camp agrees that time and trust are the two assets a process burns fastest. Transact Capital builds its Confidential Information Presentation for speed, because "time can kill deals" and fewer one-off questions mean less wasted time. The firm also uses the document to impress and qualify buyers [tqw5CWasFOU @ 00:00:27]. Sims targets a close in 3 to 6 months and sees fatigue set in at 4 to 6 months [uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:16:06]. Uhler's line is "Momentum is our friend." Both warn that data requests stretching from one month to three turn buyers off while the buyer's advisor meter keeps running. On trust, iGOTHAM says the CIM does not need to answer every question, but it must show strengths and weaknesses honestly, because hiding them "only creates distrust" [r1DSXPxZzu8 @ 00:00:48]. Parsley calls trust "probably the single most critically important" intangible in a deal. The instruction to buyers is to "cut bait" and find something else the moment a seller lies [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:35:10]. Taken together, the consensus prerequisites are three. The seller must answer fast. The offering document must disclose weaknesses before diligence finds them. And the buyer treats any discovered misstatement as grounds to reprice or walk.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: From CIM to Funded Close
paragraphs: Most practitioners run a sequence close to Patrick O'Connell's ten steps for $1M to $25M deals. Pick target industries. Source deals by emailing brokers such as Transworld or through platforms like Search Funder, Acquire.com and BizBuySell. Sign the NDA and pull P&Ls. Submit an LOI or IOI covering price, terms and 60 to 90 days of exclusivity. Then come quality-of-earnings and attorney diligence, SBA financing for deals under $5M, the purchase agreement, the close, and a 3-to-6-month seller transition [Q9DFb9qenh8 @ 00:02:30]. Parsley sharpens the LOI. Price and terms stay non-binding, but exclusivity must be binding and "spelled out crystal clear," ideally 60 to 90 days and sometimes only 20 to 30. The reason: an employee buyer at $1M can be outbid by a $3M PE offer [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:11:21]. The LOI should reference normalized working capital, carry a non-compete of five-plus years when the seller is young, and leave caps and baskets for the purchase agreement. Counsel comes in after the LOI, once preliminary diligence, the financing structure and financial verification are done. Mike Zaino adds that issues should be front-loaded at the LOI. Inexperienced opposing counsel should be walked through the terms rather than fought [76I0zKp5FM0 @ 00:09:15].

Post-close recourse is engineered through the capital stack, not just the contract. Parsley's example $1M deal runs $800K of SBA debt, $100K of buyer equity and a $100K seller note subordinated to the loan. The note carries a negotiated right to offset losses, such as a $50K warranty claim against a five-year note. On a $600K deal, a $50K to $60K loss is not worth litigating, so the note is the buyer's leverage [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:15:08]. SMB Law Group confirms the Main Street norm. Escrow is "almost never" used below the mid-market; a set-off against the promissory note replaces it, and survival terms typically run 12 to 24 months [LASFByP_8g4 @ 00:07:37]. Up market, Zaino reports indemnity caps of 10 to 20 percent, sometimes 5 percent on smaller deals. On a $10M deal, that means $0.5M to $2M held for 12 to 18 months. The money is invested conservatively and released only after written claim notices are resolved [76I0zKp5FM0 @ 00:15:14]. Rep and warranty insurance becomes common above $20M to $50M. It is usually buyer-paid and costs 25 to 50 basis points, or $250K to $500K. Ryan Smith's deposit norm is $5K to $10K, refundable and tied to a 30/60/90-day contingency.

The presentation package and the pre-listing screen are where sellers buy speed. iGOTHAM says buyers expect at least 17 coverage areas. The document opens with an executive summary and runs through transaction overview, customers, management, financial summary, competition and modeling, with financials told as a storyline rather than an afterthought [r1DSXPxZzu8 @ 00:00:00]. Transact Capital's CIP runs upwards of 50 pages, is released after the teaser and NDA, and is branded to the company [tqw5CWasFOU @ 00:00:14]. Weatherly's pre-listing review follows three steps: screen, sort, solve. It covers nine screens, from earnings quality and concentration to transferability, related parties and tax/legal. The seller then produces three years of returns tied line by line to the P&L, a receipt for every add-back, the top 10 customers over the trailing 12 months, a full debt schedule, an equipment age list and a written transition plan. Books get reconciled monthly for 12 months, and unproven add-backs come out [55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:01:47]. M&A Synergy AI pitches a generator that turns raw financials into a CIM of 100-plus slides, plus a financial model and sensitivity analysis. The vendor claims 40 hours of work cut to a 15-minute draft and 75 percent fewer diligence hours, and positions the tool as upgrading analysts rather than replacing them [h3OE0enrIxg @ 00:03:34].

callout.body: These are the small structural choices practitioners rely on to keep leverage and trust intact through diligence.
items: Write the offset right into the seller note: "it's a lot easier to negotiate those types of resolutions when you have some of the sellers money still in your pocket." [My SBA Loan Pro Podcast — VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:17:31]

For new product lines, structure the price around them instead of paying for "hockey stick" projections. [Amped Success - Matt Uhler — uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:37:45]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how much of the price a seller should leave on the table. Quiet Light Brokerage throws out "full price" LOIs that are 100% seller financed over a 10-year payout at a meager rate, such as $19,000 a month, because "there is a transfer of risk that has to happen in the deals that we do" [_t4Q9Q7VTtQ @ 00:01:13]. The seller keeps the risk without the money, those deals tend to end up in a courtroom, and the only carve-out the advisor allows is buying out a partner. Jake Parsley reaches the same verdict from the buy side, flagging 100% seller-financed deals as a warning sign, yet still wants a slice of seller paper, such as a $100K note on a $1M deal subordinated to the SBA loan, because a negotiated offset right turns that note into leverage [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:26:32]. The real divergence is post-close recourse by deal size. SMB Law Group says escrow is "almost never" used on Main Street, where market is a set-off against the promissory note [LASFByP_8g4 @ 00:07:37]. Mike Zaino runs mid-market indemnity off escrow instead, with caps of 10-20%, sometimes 5% on smaller deals, and $0.5-2M held for 12-18 months on a $10M deal, invested conservatively until claims resolve [76I0zKp5FM0 @ 00:15:14].

Practitioners also split on how much cash and lawyer time to burn before diligence proves the deal. Ryan Smith runs a $5-10K refundable deposit tied to a 30/60/90-day contingency, while Jake Parsley prefers no deposit at all and would rather see that money spent on diligence; a 10% deposit weakens buyer leverage, and Parsley watched a $20K earnest-money fight go to litigation, though some sellers make it pay to play, as on a $2M HVAC deal [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:19:56]. On counsel timing, Parsley tells cost-conscious buyers to handle NDAs and LOIs themselves with a free template and engage an attorney only after the LOI, once preliminary diligence is done, financing is structured and financials are verified [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:06:57]. Mike Zaino pushes the other way: front-load issues at the LOI, and when the other side brings green counsel, walk them through the terms rather than letting problems surface late [76I0zKp5FM0 @ 00:09:15]. Patrick O'Connell's ten-step sequence splits the difference, calling a lawyer or M&A professional "highly recommended" at the purchase agreement, where price, non-competes and reps and warranties that limit liability get locked, and recommending 60-90 days of exclusivity at the LOI stage [Q9DFb9qenh8 @ 00:04:46].

The third fault line is whose data to trust. SMB Law Group treats the 134-page ABA private M&A deal point study as the gold standard, but warns that "the number one way I see dealpoint studies and market data go wrong in a negotiation is an inexperienced lawyer relying on the deal point studies and not understanding why" [LASFByP_8g4 @ 00:28:58]; market is a range drawn from similarly situated deals, and the firm refused a PE demand that showed up in only 3% of deals. Quiet Light Brokerage ignores external "down 35%" headlines and prices off its own close reports, 40-45 questions per deal across 100-125 closings a year, which the advisor calls 98-99% accurate [ow7ewDogN14 @ 00:03:00]. AI splits the field hardest. M&A Synergy AI pitches a generator that turns a 40-hour CIM job into a 15-minute draft and cuts diligence hours 75%, positioned as upgrading analysts rather than replacing them [h3OE0enrIxg @ 00:03:34]. Mark Sims counters that AI is garbage in, garbage out, and that without one version of the truth two people will hand a buyer two different August sales figures, net versus gross [uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:31:12]. SMB Law Group adds that AI and Claude prompts can mislead clients.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common way a good deal dies is in the numbers. Charles Weatherly lists the killers as unverifiable add-backs, financials that don't tie to tax returns, and owner dependence; once the buyer finds them, the price gets recut in the buyer's favor or the buyer walks, and relistings rarely come back at the same price [55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:00:01]. Concentration is the trap that can't be patched on deadline: one customer at 38% of revenue can't be fixed "in 60 days" [55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:04:32]. Mark Sims watched a $300M-revenue client turn out to be five businesses that had never been integrated, so the buyer would not pay full price, and Matt Uhler has seen $300,000 bookkeeper mistakes [uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:13:01]. The economics check cuts deeper than the error itself: an ongoing cost becomes a haircut on value, a one-time cost comes straight off the purchase price, and Uhler reports that buyers often deduct more than the fix actually costs. On the presentation side, iGOTHAM warns that hiding weaknesses in the CIM "only creates distrust," and Weatherly frames a problem the buyer discovers at week six as broken trust [r1DSXPxZzu8 @ 00:00:48].

The second failure mode is time, and several practitioners price it explicitly. Mark Sims targeted a 3-6 month close, saw fatigue set in at 4-6 months, and watched data requests that should take one month stretch to three while the buyer's advisor meter kept running [uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:08:07]; Matt Uhler's rule is "momentum is our friend." Transact Capital builds a 50-plus-page CIP precisely because "time can kill deals," and fewer one-off buyer questions means less wasted time [tqw5CWasFOU @ 00:00:27]. Messy paperwork compounds the clock. Mike Zaino's pre-sale cleanup list starts with intellectual property sitting with the founder instead of the company entity, then runs through unpapered ownership promises such as a 5% stake, consents from minority holders and landlords, and lease renewal rights, all prepared "before engaging with buyers so that we know what we can deliver" [76I0zKp5FM0 @ 00:06:18]. The economics bite on bigger buyers too: Sims notes a PE platform that spends its first year fixing systems is hurting its own deal thesis, and bad data shows up as multiple erosion. The Carter Morse & Goodrich seller, who started from zero, said the process ran harder and longer than expected and would get finances buttoned down before engaging a bank next time [a71tQJb9UFE @ 00:01:08].

The third trap is trusting the counterparty before verifying it. Shane Pogue pulled county and assessor records and ordered mortgage documents on a sponsor's track record and found only one property legitimate; the sponsor had hidden a co-GP role, and a "Kansas" apartment was a mirrored image of a Houston building [0Z2XoqRkE00 @ 00:11:17]. Pogue's tell for Ponzi schemes tied to real businesses is financial stress, which can usually be spotted beforehand, and the fix is continual diligence such as verifying loan volume, built out before it is needed. The OOIDA Foundation puts double brokering at an estimated $500-700M in freight a year and tells carriers that a broker never needs a photo ID, that any SAFER mismatch with the broker-carrier agreement is a red flag, and that a mid-route delivery change means calling the shipper direct [XuAjQG6VmJg @ 00:00:02]. Jake Parsley's rule on a lying seller is blunt: "cut bait cut bait on that deal and get out of there and find something else" [VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:35:10]. Peter Lehrman says missing reputation between counterparties breaks deals, and tells independent sponsors that proof of work is the answer: one closed deal cancels the better-capitalized advantage, and references should be offered rather than hidden [8mBk6b5QR5I @ 00:12:08].

callout.title: Kill-or-Proceed Checks Before Signing
callout.body: Run these four checks before the purchase agreement gets signed; each one maps to a deal the practitioners watched die, get recut, or turn into a fight.
items: Tie three years of tax returns to the P&L line by line and strip any add-back without a receipt before going to market [CHARLES WEATHERLY — 55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:01:47].

Reject 100% seller-financed "full price" LOIs unless it is a partner buyout, because no risk transfer means the seller holds the risk without the money [Quiet Light Brokerage — _t4Q9Q7VTtQ @ 00:01:13].

Keep part of the seller's money in your pocket through a seller note with an offset right, since a $50-60K loss on a $600K deal is not worth litigating [My SBA Loan Pro Podcast — VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:23:06].
Turn data requests around inside the month, because stretching from one month to three turns buyers off while their advisor meter keeps running [Amped Success - Matt Uhler — uG64e1KV1S0 @ 00:09:26].

action_checklist: Run the nine pre-listing screens (earnings quality, owner dependence, concentration, debt coverage, working capital and capex, proof, transferability, related parties, tax and legal) before the deal goes to market [CHARLES WEATHERLY — 55kqfOfgIZw @ 00:01:10].

Structure a seller note subordinated to the SBA loan and negotiate a right to offset losses against it, such as a $50K warranty claim against a 5-year note [My SBA Loan Pro Podcast — VaF6Cv0koYQ @ 00:16:42].
Build the CIM with an executive summary up front, financials told as a storyline, and weaknesses shown honestly rather than hidden [iGOTHAM — r1DSXPxZzu8 @ 00:00:48].
